lesson.title: The Event Horizon: Why More Power Cannot Help
lesson.objective: Explain why neither a stronger rocket nor an outward-directed light beam can escape from inside an event horizon.
lesson.approachReason: Testing the belief that enough power can overcome any gravitational pull reveals that an event horizon is a limit on possible escape paths, not merely a region of strong gravity.

blocks.heading: The problem is the route, not the power
blocks.body:
It is tempting to imagine a black hole as a gravitational obstacle that a sufficiently powerful engine could overcome. But inside its event horizon, there is no outward escape route available—even to light.

The event horizon is the boundary separating events that can send signals to the distant exterior from those that cannot. For this lesson, picture a simple, nonrotating black hole: inside its horizon, every possible future path of a spacecraft or light signal leads toward smaller radius. Pointing a beam outward does not give it a path back outside.
blocks.example: “Outward” describes where you aim. It does not guarantee that the signal can reach a larger radius.

hints: Ask whether the problem is too little thrust or the absence of an escape route.
Light already follows the fastest routes available to a signal.
blocks.retry: A stronger engine can change which allowed path a rocket follows. It cannot create an escape path where none exists.

blocks.heading: A boundary, not a wall
blocks.body:
The horizon is not a solid shell that catches light, and light does not locally slow to a stop there. Someone measuring a nearby light beam still measures the usual speed of light.

What changes is where that beam can go. Outside the horizon, an appropriately directed light beam can escape; inside, none can. In our idealized, unchanging black hole, light directed exactly outward at the horizon stays on the horizon rather than reaching the distant exterior.
blocks.example: The limit concerns communication with the outside—not whether a flashlight can shine locally.

hints: Compare the locations of emission before comparing the brightness of the beams.
Outside the horizon, some light paths lead away. Inside, no light path leads back outside.
blocks.retry: Increasing a beam’s brightness changes how much light is emitted, not whether an escape route exists.

blocks.heading: Replace the original explanation
blocks.prompt: A friend says, “Light cannot escape because the horizon is a wall that stops it. A powerful enough rocket could punch through.” In two sentences, replace both parts of that explanation with a better one.
blocks.model: The horizon is not a material wall, and light still travels at its usual speed when measured locally. Inside the horizon, no allowed future path leads back outside, so neither light nor a more powerful rocket can escape.

activities.title: Turn up the laser
activities.prompt: In this imagined experiment, a probe has crossed inside a black hole’s event horizon. It aims a laser outward toward a distant receiver. If it makes the laser much brighter, what happens?
activities.reveal: Even the brighter beam cannot escape. Brightness changes the amount of light, not the available paths through spacetime.

options.text: Enough brightness lets the beam break through the horizon.
options.feedback: The horizon is not a barrier that extra light energy can punch through.

options.text: The beam escapes, but it takes longer than a dim beam.
options.feedback: The issue is not the travel time: no escape path exists from inside.

options.text: Neither the dim beam nor the brighter beam reaches the distant receiver.
options.feedback: Correct. Once emitted inside, neither beam has a route back outside.

activities.title: Where can an outward signal go?
activities.prompt: Tap the three emission locations and trace their connections. This is a map of possible destinations, not a picture of curved light rays. Use our idealized, unchanging, nonrotating black hole.
activities.reveal: The horizon marks the dividing line: outside it, escape is possible; inside it, even outward-directed light must move toward smaller radius.

nodes.label: Outside the horizon
nodes.detail: An appropriately directed outward light beam can reach the distant exterior.

nodes.label: Exactly on the horizon
nodes.detail: The limiting outward light path stays on the horizon in this idealized, unchanging black hole.

nodes.label: Inside the horizon
nodes.detail: Even light aimed outward follows a future path toward smaller radius. A spacecraft cannot do better.

nodes.label: Distant exterior
nodes.detail: An escaping signal can reach a receiver far from the black hole.

nodes.label: Smaller radius inside
nodes.detail: Inside this nonrotating black hole, moving toward smaller radius is unavoidable for light and spacecraft.

edges.label: All future signal paths lead inward

questions.question: A spacecraft is already inside the event horizon. Its pilot aims away from the black hole and switches on a much stronger engine. Why can the spacecraft still not escape?
options: The horizon is a solid surface that blocks the spacecraft.
There is no allowed future path from its location back outside.
Its engine must first make the spacecraft brighter than a laser.
Escape is possible if the pilot waits for gravity to stop pulling.
questions.correctAnswer: There is no allowed future path from its location back outside.
questions.explanation: Inside the horizon, even light has no path back outside. More thrust cannot give a spacecraft a route that light itself cannot take.

questions.question: Two probes aim light signals outward toward a distant receiver. Probe A emits just outside the horizon; probe B emits just inside it with a much brighter laser. Which statement is correct?
options: Only B’s signal can arrive, because brightness overcomes gravity.
Both signals must arrive, because light always moves locally at the same speed.
Neither signal can arrive, because a horizon blocks all nearby light.
A’s signal can escape; B’s cannot, regardless of its brightness.
questions.correctAnswer: A’s signal can escape; B’s cannot, regardless of its brightness.
questions.explanation: An outward escape route exists outside the horizon, but none exists inside it. The local speed and brightness of light do not remove that distinction.

problems: The central explanation correctly states that all future paths inside the horizon lead inward, but mostly asserts this rather than building an intuitive understanding of why spacetime permits no escape route.

The diagram activity is largely passive: tapping nodes reveals information, but the learner does not predict or construct connections. The exactly-on-the-horizon node also has no edge representing its stated destination.
The first check has implausible distractors about spacecraft brightness and waiting for gravity to stop, reducing its diagnostic value.
The retry explanations mostly repeat the original route-versus-power explanation rather than offering a genuinely different explanatory approach.
